title: Keep the door open (6:3)
hook: like Pharaoh, a person can close the door of return through repeated wrong
tomorrow: is it enough to fix what you did, or also who you are?

segments.voice: Yesterday: beyond our knowing. God knows, a person chooses, and how both are true is past our reach. Today, what happens to a choice made the same way again and again.
screen: `BEYOND OUR KNOWING.` → `THE SAME CHOICE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: A door that isn't used starts to stick. Paint seals the edge, the hinge stiffens, and one day it takes a shoulder to move it. Can a door close so long it won't open again? Maimonides answers with the hardest case he can find, a king who kept saying no.
screen: `A DOOR THAT ISN'T USED STICKS.` → `A KING WHO KEPT SAYING NO.`

segments.voice: In chapter six he writes that a person can do wrong so greatly, or so often, that return is withheld from them, and they aren't given the room to turn. His example is Pharaoh. The Torah says, "I will harden Pharaoh's heart." Maimonides reads it this way: Pharaoh did wrong first, on his own, again and again, and the hardening came at the end of that road, not at the beginning. It's a warning about how habits set, not a verdict on anyone listening. And the same book insists, earlier, that nothing stands in the way of a real return. So the lesson is practical. The door opens most easily while it's still in use. Look back at this week. Even after death. One deed tips the world. Wake up, sleepers. Clear the path. Free to choose. Beyond our knowing. Each one is a way of using the door: naming a wrong, doing one deed, waking up, clearing the floor, choosing on purpose. Keep the door open.
screen: `RETURN CAN BE WITHHELD.` · `PHARAOH CHOSE FIRST.` · `NOTHING STANDS IN THE WAY.` · `A WEEK OF USING THE DOOR.` · then, large: `KEEP THE DOOR OPEN.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms open and facing up, the posture of a door left ajar. Bring to mind one relationship or habit where the hinge has started to stiffen. Keep your hands open, and stay with it until the bell.
Keep the door open: Maimonides' warning from Pharaoh. Repeated wrong can close the way back, so turn while turning is still easy.
Hold onto this: keep the door open, because a door in use doesn't stick. Two weeks of return, and more ahead.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on return stresses turning while turning is still easy; the Pharaoh passages of Exodus are read in synagogue each year, and Maimonides' reading of the hardened heart is a classic text on habit and choice.

chat.meaning: Doors stick when they aren't used. Maimonides warns how habits harden; keep turning toward each other and the door stays open.

Pharaoh.meaning: Egypt's king in Exodus, whose heart was hardened

Torah.meaning: the Five Books of Moses; also all Jewish teaching

Maimonides.meaning: medieval rabbi and philosopher; wrote the Laws of Return

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 6:3 (return withheld after great or repeated wrong; Pharaoh)

notes: Hilkhot Teshuvah 6:3 paraphrased ('monin mimenu ha-teshuvah'). The voice frames it as a warning about habit, not a verdict on any listener, and pairs it with 3:14 ('ein lecha davar she'omed bifnei ha-teshuvah'). Confirm both and the framing; this is theologically sensitive.
'The hardening came at the end of that road': Maimonides says Pharaoh sinned first of his own will; Exodus has Pharaoh harden his own heart in the earlier plagues. Confirm wording.
howItsDone: the Exodus Torah portions (Va'era, Bo) are read in the annual cycle. Confirm.
